source: Donohue, van Gelder, Cumming, Bissett (2002) Reason! Project Studies 1999-2002, Technical Report 2002/1
finding: Founding pre/post data for the Reason!Able argument-mapping course at Melbourne. Gains on the CCTST were large across three cohorts. There was no randomised control group.
numbers: CCTST d (manual SD 4.457): 2000 n=50 d=0.89; 2001 n=114 d=0.89 (raw gain 3.98, pre 18.11, post 22.09); 2002 n=117 d=0.73. Written essay markers: d 0.5 to 1.13. WGCTA 1999 prototype n=53 d=0.39.
quote: Students in subjects using the Reason! approach improved with an effect size of approximately 0.8
limits: Pre/post only, same teacher team, one university. The 0.8 gain is on the CCTST, a multiple-choice test close to the practice material.
agent_relevance: Argument mapping gives a large but uncontrolled gain on structured reasoning tests. It is a task-class skill claim, not a general one.

source: Donohue et al. (2002) Reason! Project Technical Report: comparison and baseline courses
finding: Traditional critical thinking teaching and ordinary first-year study produced small gains on the same tests.
numbers: Traditional P003 1999 (WGCTA, n=46) d=0.02. Monash philosophy 2001 n=61 d=0.32 (CI -0.05 to 0.69, not significant). Monash 6-week philosophy plus 6-week CT n=174 d=0.27. HPS Melbourne n=42 d=0.37 (CI -0.14 to 0.88). Authors estimate about 0.2 per semester with no CT study.
limits: Different cohorts, tests and teachers, so not a randomised contrast. Comparison groups are small and some intervals are wide.
agent_relevance: The useful contrast is mapping versus ordinary CT teaching. An agent test needs a plain free-text reasoning control, not a no-reasoning control.

source: Donohue et al. (2002) Reason! Project Technical Report: follow-up, practice dose, ceiling
finding: Gain persisted in a small follow-up, rose with hours of practice, and was larger for weak starters. The authors warn that regression and ceiling may inflate this.
numbers: Follow-up more than 9 months later, self-selected n=20: pre 19.30, post 23.70, follow-up 23.70, d=0.75. 2002 cohort (N=50): high users gain 5.17 (SD 4.36) vs low users 2.38 (SD 3.19), split at median 8.84 hours. Correlation of pre-test and gain r=-0.54, N=281.
limits: Follow-up sample tiny and self-selected. Dose-response is correlational. The negative pre-test/gain correlation can come from regression to the mean.
agent_relevance: Practice amount and starting level moderate the gain. For an agent: more attempts help most on a weak baseline; a strong baseline gains less.

source: van Gelder, Bissett, Cumming (2004) Cultivating expertise in informal reasoning, Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology
finding: Two cohorts took a 12-week Reason!Able mapping course. Gain was large. Computer-logged practice predicted gain only weakly.
numbers: Mean gain d=0.80 (95% CI 0.66-0.94), CCTST pre 18.82, post 22.40, t(231)=14.08, p<.001. Practice correlations with gain about r=0.3 (hours r=.31); six practice variables explained 20% of gain variance. Authors estimate about 0.3 SD would come anyway, so about 0.5 SD extra.
quote: The average effect size, across the two cohorts, was 0.8.
limits: Quasi-experimental, no control group. No moderator reached significance (academic ability, prior CT, collaboration, tutor help). Correlations were lower than predicted.
agent_relevance: Best effect size after removing maturation is about 0.5 SD, not 0.8. Plan agent expectations from the lower figure.

source: van Gelder, Bissett, Cumming (2004), maturation baselines
finding: The authors compare their gain with baselines for ordinary college growth to decide how much is due to mapping.
numbers: Lehmann 1963 first-year growth 0.67 SD (0.34 per semester). Hatcher cohorts 0.55 SD per year (0.28 per semester) on the CCTST. 0.8 SD means moving from the 50th to the 79th percentile.
limits: Baselines come from other populations. The discount is an estimate, not a measured control.
agent_relevance: A fair comparison needs a baseline run on the same items. For an agent, measure the no-map arm instead of assuming it.

source: Twardy (2004) Argument Maps Improve Critical Thinking, Teaching Philosophy
finding: A sceptical outside group (Monash) swapped in a novice teacher using the Reason! method. Gain was close to the Melbourne founder's.
numbers: Monash first-year class d about 0.72 vs the founder's about 0.8 (90% of the founder gain). Typical other CT courses about 0.3; McMaster CT subject about 0.5; first year of university 0.34.
quote: computer-based argument mapping greatly enhances student critical thinking, more than tripling absolute gains made by other methods
limits: Single teacher who is also the author. Same CCTST test. No randomisation. Shared materials may keep some founder effect.
agent_relevance: The method transferred to a novice teacher, so it is not only a founder effect. Good sign for a scaffold that a weaker model can run from a fixed procedure.

source: Butchart, Forster, Gold, Bigelow, Korb, Oppy, Serrenti (2009) Improving critical thinking using web based argument mapping exercises with automated feedback, AJET
finding: A different Australian group built its own mapping tool with automatic feedback. The gain was real but about half the Melbourne size, and mapping without feedback gave little.
numbers: Mapping with automated feedback n=43 d=0.45 (CI +/-0.29), mean gain 13.7%. Standard course n=65 d=0.19. Mapping without feedback n=41 d=0.22. AOMT dispositions exercises n=49 d=0.14. Peer Instruction n=40 d=0.40. Difference from Melbourne 0.35 SD (95% CI 0.026-0.675).
quote: improvement in critical thinking scores of 0.45 standard deviations is more than 4 times greater than the 0.1 estimate
limits: Different semesters, not randomised, small samples. Authors say no reliable causal inference. Tool was less flexible (select text, no free boxes, no editing). Students mostly worked alone.
agent_relevance: Feedback on the map is the active part. Mapping alone nearly equals a plain course. A scaffold needs a checker for each map, not just a map step.

source: Butchart et al. (2009), reasons for the smaller effect and rival methods
finding: The authors list why their effect was below 0.8: tool flexibility, pair work at Melbourne, and hours of practice. Peer Instruction in lectures did about as well as mapping with feedback.
numbers: Peer Instruction d=0.40 vs automated mapping d=0.45. Pascarella and Terenzini estimate three years of college at 0.55 SD. Fullerton CT course (Facione 1990) 0.32; no-instruction Fullerton 0.14; McMaster LEMUR course (Hitchcock 2004) 0.49.
limits: Explanations are offered by the authors without testing.
agent_relevance: Good teaching or collaboration may rival mapping. For agents, a second independent critic may add as much as the map itself.

source: Dwyer, Hogan, Stewart (2011) PhD thesis, The Evaluation of Argument Mapping as a Learning Tool, Study 2: map vs hierarchical outline vs control
finding: Six-week CT training taught with argument mapping did not beat the same course taught with plain hierarchical outlines. Both beat no training on some subskills.
numbers: Study 2 N=81 first-year psychology students. AM beat control on inductive reasoning; HO did too; AM vs HO no difference. AM did not raise overall CT or reflective judgement over HO or control. AM and HO combined beat control on analysis, evaluation and inductive reasoning.
quote: the hierarchical organisation of propositions within AMs and HOs may be the critical feature
limits: Small groups, six weeks, limited instructor feedback, low engagement. Authors blame these for the null result.
agent_relevance: Key competing explanation: hierarchical structure may carry the benefit, not the box-and-arrow diagram. An outline scaffold may do as well for an agent and cost less.

source: Dwyer, Hogan, Stewart (2011) PhD thesis, Study 1 recall experiments
finding: Reading or building argument maps improved immediate recall of an argument's propositions versus text reading or summarising. Colour did not matter. Maps did not beat outlines.
numbers: Experiments used first-year psychology students (N=131, N=136, N=81; delayed recall N=199, immediate N=286). AM reading beat text reading across colour or monochrome, setting and topic. AM and HO construction beat text summarisation; AM vs HO no difference.
limits: Immediate recall mainly. Laboratory materials. Recall of an argument is not reasoning quality.
agent_relevance: Structured layout helps hold an argument in view, which may help long-context work. It does not show better reasoning.

source: Dwyer, Hogan, Stewart (2012) An evaluation of argument mapping as a method of enhancing critical thinking performance in e-learning environments, Metacognition and Learning (Study 3 of thesis)
finding: Eight-week e-learning course with mapping versus a no-instruction control. The mapping group gained more overall and on argument analysis. Problem-solving did not improve more than control.
numbers: 74 completed (AM course n=43, control n=31), Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment. AM group improved pre to post on overall CT and all five subscales; beat control on overall CT, argument analysis and verbal reasoning. High-engagement group gained more on problem-solving. No change in motivation or need for cognition.
limits: Control was no instruction, not an active alternative. Dropouts reduced the post-test sample. Short course.
agent_relevance: Mapping helps argument analysis and verbal reasoning, not general problem-solving. Scope the map step to argument-shaped tasks.

source: Alvarez-Ortiz (2007) meta-analysis of undergraduate CT instruction, as reported in the Dwyer (2011) thesis
finding: Meta-analysis of 52 studies. Courses with some explicit CT beat courses with none. Courses with a lot of argument-mapping practice (LAMP) had the highest effect.
numbers: Some CT taught 0.30 SD (CI .16-.43); no explicit CT 0.12 SD (CI .08-.17); philosophy courses 0.26 SD (CI .12-.39) vs other courses 0.16 SD; courses with at least some mapping 0.68 SD (CI .51-.86); LAMP 0.78 SD (CI .67-.89); computer-supported CT training 0.49 SD. Only 29 of 52 studies taught CT; 12 used dedicated CT.
quote: Courses with some CT taught: 0.30 SD; with no CT: 0.12 SD
limits: Second-hand through the Dwyer thesis. The LAMP effect was built from Donohue 2002, Butchart 2009, Twardy 2004 and van Gelder 2000-2001, which is the same advocate cluster, and Dwyer notes each had methodological flaws. The unpublished thesis itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: The 0.78 is not independent of the founding studies. Use 0.3 (general CT) and 0.5 to 0.8 (mapping) as a range with a wide error.

source: Dwyer, Hogan, Stewart (2012) Metacognition and Learning repository abstract page
finding: Search snippet repeated the abstract: mapping course gained overall and on all subscales pre to post, and beat controls on overall CT and argument analysis. Post-test CT correlated with motivation and need for cognition.
numbers: 74 undergraduate psychology students, 8-week intervention, Halpern assessment.
limits: Opened only through a search snippet. Numbers confirmed in the thesis (see earlier line).
agent_relevance: Dispositions correlate with performance. An agent has no motivation, so the analogue is how much effort budget it spends.

source: Harrell (2008) No computer program required: even pencil-and-paper argument mapping improves critical-thinking skills, Teaching Philosophy
finding: Pencil-and-paper diagramming in an introductory philosophy course improved CCTST gains, with the biggest gains for students who actually built maps. Known only from secondary summaries.
numbers: Exact numbers not obtained (PDF blocked). Secondary source: all students improved; largest gains among students who constructed argument maps.
limits: Not read. The Chang et al. (2025) scoping review describes this study as 180 students in English translation courses using Rationale, which conflicts with the pencil-and-paper title, so that description looks wrong.
agent_relevance: Software is not required. A written two-column map in the prompt may be enough for an agent.

source: Harrell (2011) Argument diagramming and critical thinking in introductory philosophy, Higher Education Research and Development
finding: Argument diagramming significantly improved argument analysis for low and intermediate achievers. The abstract notes methodological problems in earlier studies. High achievers were not shown to benefit.
numbers: Exact effect sizes not obtained. Treatment group taught diagramming; control group not.
limits: Seen only as an abstract fragment in a search result. Confirm before citing numbers.
agent_relevance: Gains concentrate in weaker starters, matching the Reason! ceiling result. A strong model may gain least.

source: Doctoral dissertation on Rationale-based mapping with MANCOVA on CCTST-2000 (found by search, author and year unknown)
finding: Null result: an intervention using Rationale software showed no significant effect of intervention method on post-test CCTST.
numbers: MANCOVA: no significant relationship between intervention method and post-test critical thinking. MANOVA: no significant effect on CCTST-2000 subscales. N not obtained.
limits: Seen only as a search snippet. The PDF could not be downloaded. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Null results exist. Do not assume the 0.8 effect holds for every course and tool.

source: Chang, Lin, Hwang (2025) Charting the field: a review of argument visualization research for writing, learning, and reasoning, Frontiers in Education
finding: Scoping review of post-secondary argument visualisation studies. Evidence is mostly quasi-experimental, concentrated in language learning, and based on achievement tests. Not a meta-analysis.
numbers: 45 studies; 34 quasi-experimental; Rationale used in 10; achievement tests in 15, map reproduction in 9, essays in 7. Most common subject EFL (8), education (6), philosophy (3), business (3). Authors say pooled meta-analysis is impractical now.
limits: No pooled effect sizes. Possible bias toward positive reports. One misdescription of Harrell 2008 noticed.
agent_relevance: The field has few randomised designs. Treat claims as moderate evidence, scoped to a task class.

source: Chang et al. (2025) scoping review: study sizes and tool training
finding: Studies outside philosophy use mapping mainly as pre-writing planning, with positive but mostly perception-based findings. Training on the tool and on argument schemes is often missing.
numbers: Examples: EFL essay support n=201; TESOL pre-writing n=28; business education n=291 (Carrington 2011); collaborative map n=17; medical diagnostic reasoning n=29 (Wu 2013). 16 studies gave no tool training.
limits: Outcomes mostly perception or essay scores. Study descriptions second-hand.
agent_relevance: Mapping as a planning step before generating text is the closest human analogue to an agent's Represent step. Teach the scheme, not just the tool.

source: Systematic review: Argument Mapping in Higher Education, Higher Education Quarterly (2025)
finding: Systematic review coded 124 argument-map studies. Aim included judging readiness for a meta-analysis.
numbers: 124 studies coded; 102 empirical; 44% studied attitudes; 40% collaborative mapping; 51% map quality or structure. Effect of mapping on critical thinking was the most frequent causal question.
limits: Abstract only, read through OpenAlex. Publisher page blocked.
agent_relevance: Most mapping research studies attitudes and map quality, not performance on new tasks.

source: Systematic review: Argument mapping improves critical thinking skills (2026, Routledge chapter)
finding: A 2026 systematic review pooled argument-mapping pre/post studies over 34 years and reports a large pooled effect, with admitted heterogeneity.
numbers: 86 usable documents (56 journal articles, 27 conference papers, 1 chapter); effect sizes as Cohen d, Glass delta and Hedges g; pooled effect described as large. No numeric pooled value obtained.
limits: Abstract only. Mixed effect-size types and conference papers included.
agent_relevance: Ask whether the pooled effect falls under quality weighting. Use the lower 0.5 SD figure until the paper is read.

source: Davies, Barnett, van Gelder (2015) Using computer-aided argument mapping to teach reasoning, in Studies in Critical Thinking
finding: Advocate summary: high-intensity mapping courses improve critical thinking by about 0.8 SD, more than twice a standard CT course. Notes mapping can be done without software.
numbers: 0.8 SD for high-intensity courses; standard CT courses about 0.3 SD.
limits: Written by developers of the method. Only the introduction was read.
agent_relevance: Treat 0.8 as the advocates' upper figure. Hold 0.3 to 0.5 as a planning range.

source: Narra (2026) Pedagogic applications of argument maps to enhance critical thinking, TeachNLP 2026
finding: Short teaching report on mapping in a Finnish master's writing course and a project course. Only feedback comments, no test scores.
numbers: No effect sizes. Voluntary end-of-course survey with positive comments. Students were allowed to depart from mapping rules.
limits: Anecdotal, no control, self-selected survey. Not evidence of improvement.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Listed to show that the 2026 literature includes uncontrolled reports.

source: Unpublished or thesis-level study: guided practice with computer-assisted argument mapping, high-school sophomores, University of South Carolina (2020)
finding: One-group pre/post study of high-school students using computer-assisted argument maps for analysis and composition. Large gain, no control.
numbers: N=71, t=7.71, d=0.91 on composite map scores.
limits: No control group. The outcome is performance on maps themselves, close to the training task. Cannot exclude practice or maturation.
agent_relevance: Example of the common weak design. Gains on map-making are not gains on transfer tasks.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification, AAAI
finding: ArgLLMs build a small argument graph (claim, a supporter, an attacker; depth 1 or 2) and compute claim strength by formal semantics. Accuracy was not better than direct or chain-of-thought answers, but the result can be contested by editing the graph.
numbers: Three datasets (TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim), seven models plus GPT-4o. Examples: GPT-4o 0.85 direct, 0.85 CoT, 0.83 ArgLLM (depth 1, estimated base) on MedClaim; plain 0.5 base-score ArgLLM was usually 0.03 to 0.10 below CoT. Depth 2 usually no better than depth 1.
quote: even powerful models have relatively limited zero-shot capabilities in argument generation and estimation
limits: Zero-shot argument generation. The authors say even strong models are limited here and suggest fine-tuning. Binary claim verification only. Some table row labels were lost in text extraction.
agent_relevance: A map-based decision step costs little accuracy and gives an audit trail a user can change. Do not expect it to raise accuracy alone.

source: Ng, Jiang, Freedman, Rago, Toni (2025) MArgE: Meshing Argumentative Evidence from Multiple LLMs for Justifiable Claim Verification, arXiv 2508.02584
finding: Combine argument trees from three small models, scored by a stronger model. Beats unstructured multi-LLM debate and ensembles of single ArgLLMs.
numbers: Three open models (4B to 8B) plus GPT-4o mini scorer. With the stronger scorer, gains up to about 20% over comparison methods; beats GPT-4o mini CoT on two of three datasets by 3.5% and 1.0%; less accurate on MedClaim. Debate configurations on one set ranged 0.676 to 0.808 accuracy. Depth 1 better than depth 2 with estimated arguments.
limits: Claim verification only. Gains depend on the scorer, not the map alone. Mean of three runs.
agent_relevance: A tree is a better merge format than free debate when combining several samples.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Evaluating uncertainty quantification methods in Argumentative LLMs, Findings of EMNLP
finding: Inside an ArgLLM argument graph, plain direct prompting for argument confidence works better than more complex uncertainty methods.
numbers: Claim verification with TruthfulQA-derived claims. Direct prompting outperformed considerably more complex methods. Exact numbers not recorded.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: A simple confidence ask per map node may be enough; do not over-engineer calibration inside a map.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Advancing fact-checking for LLMs via argumentative reasoning (ArgCheck, MAVEN benchmark), EMNLP
finding: Model claim and web evidence as arguments with attack links, resolve by grounded semantics, then ask a judge. Beats the strongest baseline on two benchmarks.
numbers: Macro-F1 above the strongest baseline by 5.39 points on MAVEN and 11.10 points on AVeriTeC.
limits: Read abstract and first figure only. The gain also comes from adversarial retrieval of pro and con evidence, not only from the graph.
agent_relevance: Mapping plus balanced retrieval of both sides gives the gain. Test the two parts separately.

source: Baur, Honda, Samek, Ma (2026) Argument Graph Uncertainty: quantifying uncertainty from the logical structure of reasoning chains, arXiv 2610.20328
finding: Turn a chain-of-thought trace into an argument graph with an entailment model and use graph structure to rate confidence. Best on GPQA for most models and complementary to sampling consistency.
numbers: Nine reasoning models on GPQA Diamond: highest PRR in 8 of 9. Nemotron-3 Nano 30B PRR 0.65 vs consistency 0.24 vs token 0.41; GPT-OSS 120B 0.56 vs 0.36 vs -0.27; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B consistency 0.46 beat graph 0.34. Blend of graph and consistency improved PRR by 0.10 on MMLU-Pro and 0.09 on TruthfulQA over the stronger part.
limits: Multiple-choice only. Segmentation is the main source of variance (paragraph split mean PRR 0.47 vs 0.46 with Qwen3-8B segmenter; larger segmenter 0.50).
agent_relevance: A map built after the fact from the agent's own reasoning can flag when to distrust an answer. Fits a verify state in the schema.

source: Li et al. (2025) Large Language Models in Argument Mining: A Survey, arXiv 2506.16383
finding: Survey says manual argument annotation is labour-intensive and unscalable, which motivates LLM extraction of argument structure. Notes argument-mapping dashboards for ESG reports and legal brief tools.
numbers: Survey, no pooled numbers. Notes few studies measure argument quality inside larger pipelines.
limits: Selected sections read. It does not test whether LLM-built maps help human or model reasoning.
agent_relevance: Map extraction by LLMs is feasible. The open question is whether it improves downstream decisions.

source: Synthesis of moderators across lines b01 to b27 (this agent's summary, not a new source)
finding: What seems to matter: amount of guided practice, feedback on each map, flexible tools, starting level, and task type. Outline structure rivals map structure.
numbers: Feedback: d 0.45 with vs 0.22 without (Butchart). Practice: r about 0.3 with gain (van Gelder 2004). Starting level: r=-0.54 with gain (Reason! report). Outline vs map: no difference in recall and in most CT scores (Dwyer thesis).
limits: Cross-study synthesis with different tests and populations. Not a formal moderator analysis.
agent_relevance: Scope Represent to argument-shaped tasks, add a per-map check, include a plain-outline arm, and expect most gain where the baseline is weak.
